subject: Social Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Who Does What? Classifying Activities Around Us
periods.section_anchor: Opening narrative (Anu, Kabir and the people in their lives)
materials: Printed or projected narrative excerpt featuring Anu, Kabir and the six characters
Blank two-column classification table (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or board-drawn table with columns 'Person / Activity' and 'Purpose / Payment?'

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud or displays the narrative about Anu and Kabir's neighbours: the Air Force pilot who earns a salary, the retired BSF officer who voluntarily teaches geography and tends a garden, the parents running a garment shop, the mother in the community knitting group, and the software-engineer brother who volunteers on weekends. Students listen and jot down each person and what they do.

Students fill the two-column table individually: in column one they list each character and their activity; in column two they note whether the activity involves payment and what seems to motivate it. Two guiding questions are on the board — 'Does this person earn money from this activity?' and 'Why else might someone do it?' — and students answer them for every character.

Pairs compare their tables and identify characters where they disagree about payment or motivation. The teacher facilitates a whole-class share-out: which activities clearly involve money, which clearly do not, and which felt uncertain — recording three columns on the board as the class builds a collective first-pass classification.

Teacher draws out the central question the chapter will explore: what makes an activity 'economic' or 'non-economic', and why both kinds matter. Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'I think the difference between an economic and a non-economic activity is…' — this is their working hypothesis they will test as the chapter proceeds.

periods.section_context: Air Force pilot, BSF volunteer, garment shop, knitting group, software engineer volunteer
periods.teacher_notes: The narrative's six characters are deliberately varied — salaried work, voluntary teaching, family business, community service — so encourage students to sit with the uncertainty before resolving it. A common confusion at this stage is equating 'important' with 'paid'; the BSF officer's voluntary geography teaching often prompts students to assume it must be paid because it resembles school. Name the two motivations — money and other reasons — explicitly on the board so students can test their hypothesis in subsequent units.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Economic Activities: Terms, Forms, and the Kamlapur Visit
materials: Chapter text covering economic activity definitions and the Kavya–Kamlapur narrative
Vocabulary anchor chart (blank, to be filled on board)
Index cards or sticky notes for each student
periods.visual_aids: Board vocabulary anchor chart: Term | Definition | Example from the chapter

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's definition of economic activities — those involving money or money's worth — and builds a vocabulary chart on the board with six terms: money's worth, market, fee, salary, wage, payment in kind. For each term, students call out a definition in their own words before the teacher confirms the chapter's phrasing, keeping the register live.

Teacher narrates the Kamlapur scene: Kavya's uncle earns a monthly salary operating a bulldozer; her aunt earns a salary at the post office and an additional weekly fee for online classes; farm labourer Sahil earns a daily wage, receiving part in cash and part as mangoes — payment in kind. Students write each character's name and the payment type they receive on a separate index card, then sort the cards on their desk from 'time-based pay' to 'service-based pay' to 'non-cash pay'.

Students tackle the chapter's Think About It prompt: recall one economic activity they passed on the way to school and identify how the worker was paid. They share with a partner, then three or four students report to the class. Teacher records the payment types on the board alongside the Kamlapur examples to show the range of forms economic activity can take.

Quick application: teacher reads four new scenarios aloud (a street food vendor, a music teacher giving private lessons, a factory worker, a person receiving rice instead of cash for harvesting crops) and students hold up the index card matching the payment type. Teacher corrects misconceptions in real time, especially the common confusion between wage and salary — both are money, but one is time-period specific and the other is monthly and fixed.

periods.section_context: Kavya, Kamlapur uncle–bulldozer, aunt–post office, Sahil–wage and mangoes
periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently conflate salary and wage since both involve regular money; anchor the distinction on duration — salary is a monthly fixed amount tied to employment, wage is pay for a specific period that can change. The Kamlapur scene also shows that a single worker (the aunt) can earn via two different forms — salary and fee — which is worth pausing on. The range of real examples students bring from their commute will ground the vocabulary in their own locality.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify economic activities by identifying the form of compensation — salary, wage, fee, or payment in kind — that each involves.

periods.activity_title: Value Addition: Tracing What Skill and Effort Add to Raw Material
materials: Chapter text on Rajesh the carpenter and value addition
Simple flow-diagram worksheet (blank boxes: Raw Material → Process → Product)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: wood (₹600) → Rajesh's skill + time + effort → chair (₹1,000); gap labelled ₹400 = value added

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the carpenter flow on the board: Rajesh buys wood for ₹600, applies skill and labour, sells the finished chair for ₹1,000. Students are asked: where did the extra ₹400 come from? They write a one-sentence explanation before any class discussion — this surfaces intuitions about labour and skill before the chapter's term is introduced.

Teacher introduces the term value addition: at each stage of transforming something from one form into another, economic value is created. Students receive or draw the blank flow-diagram and are given three new examples from the chapter's Let's Explore list — a miller grinding wheat into flour, a tailor stitching cloth into a shirt, and a baker baking flour into bread. For each, they fill the three boxes and write the value added in the gap.

Students complete the chapter's Let's Explore prompt: assess which listed professions create monetary value and add two examples of their own, writing them in the flow-diagram format. Pairs then compare: do both agree that the activity at each step adds value? Teacher circulates and presses students who list activities without identifying the transformation step.

Whole-class debrief: teacher asks 'Can value addition happen without a physical product?' and invites examples like a lawyer (transforms a client's legal problem into a resolved case) or a teacher (transforms a student's ignorance into knowledge). Students revise their definition of value addition in their notebooks to include services, not only goods.

periods.section_context: Rajesh carpenter, wood–chair transformation, ₹600–₹1000 value addition
periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent confusion here is students thinking the ₹400 is profit rather than the value of skill and effort — clarify that value addition is about what labour and skill contribute to transformation, not just the monetary surplus. Pressing students to fill the flow-diagram for service examples (lawyer, doctor) guards against reducing value addition to physical manufacturing. The earlier Kamlapur characters — the aunt's online classes, Sahil's tractor work — are useful content anchors students can return to.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the process of value addition by identifying the transformation step through which skill and effort convert raw material or a problem into a higher-value product or service.

periods.activity_title: Economic vs. Non-Economic: Drawing the Boundary
periods.section_anchor: Types of Economic Activities / The Importance of Non-Economic Activities
materials: Scenario cards (printed or written on strips) — one set per pair
periods.visual_aids: Board T-chart: 'Economic Activity' | 'Non-Economic Activity' with criteria row at top

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's definition of non-economic activities: those done out of gratitude, love, care, and respect that do not generate income or wealth. The four examples from the chapter — parents cooking for the family, helping children with schoolwork, youth caring for grandparents, family members assisting with home renovation — are read aloud. Students write their own one-line definition of what makes an activity non-economic before the class discusses.

Pairs receive a set of eight scenario cards (drawn from both sections of the chapter): selling school bags in a market, a lawyer arguing a case, a mother helping with homework, a truck driver transporting goods, a child caring for a grandparent, a farmer selling produce, a family doing home renovation together, workers in a car factory. Partners sort each card under Economic or Non-Economic and write a one-phrase justification on each card.

Pairs join into groups of four and compare classifications. Where pairs disagree, groups discuss and attempt to reach consensus using the criteria: does it involve money or money's worth? The teacher circulates and targets the home-renovation card — students often split on whether unpaid family labour counts as economic — drawing out the chapter's point that non-economic activities contribute to quality of life without monetary exchange.

Whole-class convergence: teacher rebuilds the T-chart on the board using student-agreed classifications and asks: 'Does the absence of money make an activity less important?' Students write a concluding sentence in their notebook that directly answers this question, using at least one example from the chapter.

periods.section_context: Parents cooking, homework help, grandparent care, home renovation, contrast with paid activities
periods.teacher_notes: The home-renovation example is the sharpest point of confusion because families may hire workers for the same task — students may conflate the act with the paid version. Guide them back to the chapter's criterion: is this particular instance exchanged for money? The normative point — that non-economic activities carry deep social value — is the chapter's claim, so students should reach it from the sorting exercise rather than being told it first.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish economic from non-economic activities by applying the criterion of monetary exchange to concrete scenarios.

periods.activity_title: Non-Economic Activities: Their Social and Personal Value
materials: Reflection journal or blank notebook page

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the opening question: 'If something cannot be measured in money, how do we know it has value?' Students write three examples from their own family or neighbourhood of activities done purely out of care or love, without any payment. Two or three students share, and the teacher notes the range on the board — the goal is to move from abstract definition to lived instances.

Teacher leads a structured analysis of the chapter's claim: non-economic activities contribute to social welfare, personal wellbeing, and the overall quality of life. Students take two of their own examples and for each write answers to three questions from the board: (1) Who benefits? (2) What would be lost if this activity stopped? (3) Could money replace it fully? This forces students beyond recall into evaluative reasoning about the nature of the value.

Students write a short reflective essay (one substantial paragraph) arguing whether a specific non-economic activity they identified is as important to their community as a paid activity in the same domain — e.g., a parent teaching a child at home versus a paid tutor, or a family member nursing a sick relative versus a paid nurse. They must use the chapter's criteria — love, care, gratitude, social welfare — as their evidence base.

Three or four students read their paragraph aloud. Class responds using a structured prompt: 'I agree / I want to challenge / I want to add…' Teacher closes by naming the chapter's key point: the importance of an activity is not determined by whether it earns money, and both kinds of activities together sustain family and community life.

periods.section_context: Cooking, schoolwork help, grandparent care, home renovation — value without payment
periods.teacher_notes: Students at this age often equate value with price because markets are the most visible context for exchange; the three analytical questions push them to articulate what market pricing cannot capture. The reflective paragraph is designed to be drafted, peer-responded to, and closed within this unit — do not let it run into a later sitting. Encourage students to choose examples they genuinely know rather than textbook characters so the reflection is authentic.

periods.activity_title: Sevā as Non-Economic Action: Langars, Prasād, and Selfless Giving
materials: Chapter text on sevā, langars, and prasād
Think About It prompt on the board or printed
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: two columns — 'Paid Teaching (school teacher)' | 'Voluntary Teaching (Kabir's grandfather)' — filled collaboratively

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's concept of sevā — selfless service — and its definition: contributing to society without expecting anything in return. The two examples from the chapter are described: langars at gurudwaras where food is freely served to every visitor regardless of background, and the distribution of prasād at temples. Students are asked: what motivation would lead someone to spend time and resources feeding strangers for free?

Teacher poses the chapter's Think About It question: what is the difference between Kabir's grandfather voluntarily teaching neighbourhood children and a school teacher who is paid? Students work individually to fill the two-column board diagram for their own notebook, listing at least three differences and three similarities between the two situations. The columns are then filled on the board collaboratively, with students calling out their entries.

Students are asked to identify one sevā-type non-economic activity meaningful in their own family — something done freely for others out of care, gratitude, or a sense of duty. They write a brief description: who does it, for whom, and what the person and the recipients get from it that cannot be measured in money. The chapter's phrase — 'a sense of satisfaction and gratitude for what one has' — is on the board as a prompt.

Structured class discussion: teacher asks 'Does sevā require a religious context, or can it exist outside religious institutions?' Students use the chapter's examples alongside their own family examples to argue their position. Teacher draws out the chapter's implication: sevā is a social tradition embedded in Indian life broadly, expressed through religious institutions like gurudwaras and temples but also in everyday family and community practice.

periods.section_context: Sevā concept, langars at gurudwaras, prasād at temples, Kabir's grandfather volunteer teaching
periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse sevā with charity, treating it as a one-directional gift; the chapter's emphasis on 'satisfaction and gratitude for what one has' positions sevā as mutually meaningful — the giver also gains. The comparison between Kabir's grandfather and a paid teacher is productive precisely because both teach: the difference lies in motivation and exchange, not in the act itself. Where students are from traditions that practice langars or prasād, their first-hand familiarity is a rich resource.

competency_edges.competency_text: Appreciate India's traditions of inclusion and communal giving as expressed through social and religious institutions.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how sevā — as practised through langars and prasād — embodies a tradition of communal giving that transcends monetary exchange.

periods.activity_title: Community Participation: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan as Collective Non-Economic Action
materials: Chapter text on Swachh Bharat Abhiyan
periods.visual_aids: Board cause-effect map: Individual action → Collective action → Community outcome

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the section's central argument: non-economic activities gain additional significance when people act collectively. The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan is introduced as the chapter's main example — citizens individually maintaining their homes and surroundings, and also coming together to clean streets, roads, parks, and public spaces. Teacher asks: what can a group achieve in a neighbourhood that a single family cannot?

Students fill the cause-effect organiser for the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan using three questions from the board: (1) What individual actions does this initiative ask of each citizen? (2) What collective actions does it bring people together for? (3) What outcomes — for the home, neighbourhood, and nation — does the chapter say result from this? Students write specific details from the chapter text, not general statements.

Teacher introduces the chapter's Think About It prompt and students address the first two sub-questions: identify a similar community practice from their own area, and reflect on whether festival celebrations are non-economic activities. Students write their responses in their notebooks, using the chapter's criteria — no income generated, motivated by collective wellbeing — to justify their classification of the festival example.

Pairs share their community examples, then three or four are reported to the class. Teacher maps the shared examples onto the board cause-effect structure to show that the pattern — individual action → collective action → community outcome — holds across different practices and localities. Students update their cause-effect organiser to include one example from their own area.

periods.section_context: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, individual and collective cleaning, streets, parks, public spaces
periods.teacher_notes: Students often know Swachh Bharat Abhiyan by name but treat it as a government programme rather than a collective non-economic practice by citizens — press them to locate the individual and community action within it, not just the government campaign. Festival celebrations are a deliberate edge case in the Think About It prompt: some festivals involve commercial exchange (markets, paid performers) while others are purely participatory — students should reason through this rather than assume one answer. The cause-effect organiser keeps reasoning structured.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect information about social institutions and organised community practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how individual non-economic actions combine into organised community initiatives by mapping the causal chain from personal effort to collective social outcome.

periods.activity_title: Van Mahotsav and Local Programmes: Community Participation in Practice
materials: Chapter text on Van Mahotsav and the Think About It community programme prompt
Data-collection worksheet for local community programmes (one per student)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Van Mahotsav — the festival of forests — as the chapter's second named example of organised community participation: community members come together for tree plantation drives to promote awareness about the value of trees and the conservation of forests. Students are asked: how is Van Mahotsav similar to and different from the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan? They write two similarities and two differences in their notebook before discussion.

Structured comparison: teacher builds a quick table on the board with columns 'Van Mahotsav' and 'Swachh Bharat Abhiyan' and rows 'Goal', 'Who participates?', 'Individual action', 'Collective outcome'. Students call out their answers; the teacher fills the table and draws out the general principle: community participation multiplies the impact of individual non-economic action.

Students address the chapter's third Think About It sub-question — describe community programmes undertaken by their school or locality — using the data-collection worksheet. The worksheet has three columns: Programme name | Who participates? | What is the collective outcome? Students fill in at least two real examples from memory or the chapter. Where students cannot recall programmes, teacher prompts with categories: school cleanliness drives, neighbourhood tree-planting, local festival organisation.

Students write a concluding paragraph: 'A community programme I know about is [name]. It is a non-economic activity because [reason using the chapter's criteria]. Its collective outcome is [outcome], which would not be possible if only individuals acted alone.' Teacher collects the paragraph as a check of students' ability to apply the chapter's framework to a real example.

periods.section_context: Van Mahotsav, tree plantation drives, forest conservation awareness, local community programmes
periods.teacher_notes: Van Mahotsav is sometimes known to students only as a name on a calendar; anchor it to the chapter's description — community plantation drives for forest conservation — so students see it as a collective practice, not just an observance. The paragraph students write is designed to be completed within this unit; it draws on the worksheet filled in the same sitting and requires no preparation from a prior unit. The phrase 'would not be possible if only individuals acted alone' is the chapter's core claim about collective non-economic action, and checking whether students use it correctly is the diagnostic purpose of this closing task.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect information about social institutions and organised community practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret the significance of organised community participation programmes by comparing their goals, participants, and collective outcomes.

periods.activity_title: The Full Spectrum of Work: Economic Activities, Value Addition, and Community Action
periods.section_anchor: Types of Economic Activities / The Importance of Non-Economic Activities / Sevā: selfless service / The strength of community participation
materials: Chapter summary or key-term list available for reference
Blank structured-analysis worksheet with three sections
periods.visual_aids: Board framework: three domains — Economic Activities | Non-Economic Activities | Community Participation — with sub-questions under each

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the three-domain framework on the board and invites students to populate each column with examples from across the chapter: Economic Activities (salary/wage/fee/payment in kind, value addition by Rajesh), Non-Economic Activities (family care, sevā, langars), Community Participation (Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Van Mahotsav). This is a quick retrieval exercise — students call out examples while the teacher fills the board, surfacing gaps before the analysis task begins.

Students receive or draw the structured-analysis worksheet and work independently on three analytical questions: (1) Pick any two characters from the chapter — one doing an economic activity and one doing a non-economic activity. Explain what each contributes to society that the other cannot. (2) Trace value addition through one economic activity from the chapter, naming the raw input, the transformation, and what is added. (3) Choose Swachh Bharat Abhiyan or Van Mahotsav and explain why collective participation produces a result individual action alone cannot.

Students form groups of three and share their answers to question (1), seeking the most persuasive version of the argument that both economic and non-economic activities are necessary. Each group agrees on a single best answer and nominates a speaker. Teacher selects three groups to share, then draws out the chapter's organising claim: the value of work is not reducible to money.

Individual closing task: students write a three-sentence synthesis in their notebooks — 'An economic activity I would include from the chapter is [X] because it shows [aspect of economic activity]. A non-economic activity that matters as much is [Y] because [reason using chapter's criteria]. Community participation matters because [linking to Swachh Bharat or Van Mahotsav].' Teacher circulates and reads a sample of responses to confirm the three domains are connected, not treated as separate lists.

periods.section_context: Rajesh carpenter, Kamlapur characters, langars, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Van Mahotsav
periods.teacher_notes: The three analytical questions in this unit are sequenced from character-comparison (analysis of two individuals) to process-tracing (value addition) to collective-level reasoning (community participation) — this mirrors the chapter's own movement from individual to collective. A common weakness in the closing synthesis is students listing all three domains without connecting them; the three-sentence format forces a linking word between domains. The board framework at the opening names the chapter's content domains so students can navigate their notes without needing to recall which section each example came from.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a comparative explanation of economic and non-economic activities by selecting examples and articulating what each contributes that the other cannot.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect information about social institutions and organised community practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

competency.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify economic activities by identifying the form of compensation — salary, wage, fee, or payment in kind — that each involves.
assessment_items.question_text: Sahil tills land using a tractor. At the end of the day he receives some cash and a basket of mangoes in exchange for his work. Which form of compensation does Sahil receive?

options.label: A
options.text: A daily wage and payment in kind

options.label: B
options.text: A monthly salary and a fee

options.label: C
options.text: A salary and payment in kind

options.label: D
options.text: A weekly fee and a salary

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the regularity of Sahil's daily work with the fixed monthly salary structure and adds a fee, suggesting the student has not distinguished salary (monthly, employer–employee) from wage (period-specific).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies 'fee' — a term for professional advisory payment — to a manual labour context, and misidentifies the cash component as a salary rather than a wage.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly identifies payment in kind for the mangoes but mistakes the cash component for a salary, showing partial understanding of wage versus salary distinction.

competency.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the process of value addition by identifying the transformation step through which skill and effort convert raw material or a problem into a higher-value product or service.

options.label: A
options.text: The ₹400 is Rajesh's profit after covering the cost of the wood.

options.label: B
options.text: The ₹400 is the market price charged to make the chair more expensive than its raw material.

options.label: C
options.text: The ₹400 is the transport cost Rajesh paid to deliver the chair to the buyer.

options.label: D
options.text: The ₹400 represents the monetary value added by Rajesh's skill, time, and effort in transforming the wood into a chair.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Stage | What happens | Amount (₹)
Raw material | Rajesh buys wood | 600
Transformation | Rajesh shapes the wood into a chair using his skills | —
Finished product | Rajesh sells the chair | 1000
Difference | ? | 400
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find reading tables challenging may be allowed to hear the table read aloud by a peer or teacher before answering.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates value addition with business profit; the student understands there is a monetary difference but attributes it to commercial gain rather than the labour and skill contribution the chapter defines as value addition.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Attributes the price difference to arbitrary market pricing rather than to transformation through skill and effort, showing the student has not grasped that value is created by the transformation process.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a cost category (transport) not present in the chapter scenario, suggesting the student is guessing at expenditure items rather than applying the concept of value addition.

assessment_items.question_text: A mother helps her child with homework every evening. A lawyer argues a case in court and earns a fee. Identify which of these is an economic activity and which is a non-economic activity, and explain the criterion you used to decide.
expected_elements: Correctly identifies the lawyer's work as economic and the mother's homework help as non-economic.
States the criterion: economic activities involve money or money's worth; non-economic activities do not generate income or wealth.
Applies the criterion explicitly to both examples — explains why the lawyer's activity meets the criterion and why the mother's does not.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond in bullet points rather than full sentences if writing fluency is a barrier.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a comparative explanation of economic and non-economic activities by selecting examples and articulating what each contributes that the other cannot.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Types of Economic Activities / The Importance of Non-Economic Activities / Sevā: selfless service / The strength of community participation
assessment_items.question_text: Using examples from the chapter, write an explanation arguing that economic and non-economic activities are both necessary for society. Your answer must name at least one economic activity and one non-economic activity, explain what each contributes that the other cannot, and show why removing either would leave society worse off.
look_for: Names a specific economic activity from the chapter (e.g., Rajesh's carpentry, the aunt's online classes, Sahil's farm labour) and identifies the concrete contribution it makes — goods, services, income, or value addition.

Makes an explicit comparative argument: what the economic activity provides that the non-economic one cannot (material goods, livelihoods), and what the non-economic activity provides that a paid equivalent cannot (care, solidarity, sense of belonging).

competency.competency_text: Identify and explain the key elements of economic activities, including forms of compensation and the process of value addition.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the process of value addition by identifying the transformation step through which skill and effort convert raw material or a problem into a higher-value product or service.
assessment_items.task: Choose any one economic activity from your own neighbourhood — it can involve making something, growing something, repairing something, or providing a service. Draw or write a three-box flow showing: Box 1 — the raw material or starting situation; Box 2 — the transformation step, naming the skill or effort involved; Box 3 — the finished product or resolved situation and its value. Then write two sentences below the flow explaining what value was added and by whom.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Box 1: What is the starting material or situation? (e.g., raw wood, broken bicycle, an untaught skill)
Box 2: What does the worker do to it? What skill or effort do they apply?
Box 3: What is the result, and what is it worth now?
Below the flow: Write — 'The value added is ___ because ___. The person who added this value is ___ through their ___ [skill / effort / time].'
format_of_output: Two explanatory sentences below the flow
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who prefer drawing may sketch the transformation in the boxes rather than writing words; the two sentences below remain required in any language comfortable to the student.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task asks students to apply the concept of value addition — as introduced through the Rajesh carpenter example — to a self-chosen activity from their own locality, demonstrating that they can identify the transformation step and name what skill and effort contribute, not merely recall the chapter's single example.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Box 1 checks whether the student can identify a raw input or starting state. Box 2 is the diagnostic core — a student who can name the transformation and the skill involved understands value addition; a student who merely describes the product in Box 2 has not grasped the transformation concept. Box 3 and the two sentences confirm whether the student can articulate what was added and attribute it to the worker's contribution.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: student chooses a service or non-physical example (e.g., a tutor resolving a student's confusion) showing understanding that value addition extends beyond physical goods; names a specific skill (weaving, diagnosis, repair); explains the added value in terms of the chapter's concept (skill + time + effort = transformation). Weak: student lists inputs and outputs without identifying the transformation step; writes 'profit' instead of 'value added'; chooses the same carpenter example from the chapter without applying it to a new context.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map (here rendered as a three-box flow from input through transformation to outcome) is the most natural demonstration vehicle for tracing value addition because the concept is inherently sequential and causal — value is created by what happens between input and output. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu (e.g., a structured discussion prompt with written output) that similarly externalises the transformation chain.

competency.competency_text: Collect information about social institutions and organised community practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse how individual non-economic actions combine into organised community initiatives by mapping the causal chain from personal effort to collective social outcome.
assessment_items.question_text: Under the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, citizens clean their own homes and also come together to clean streets, roads, and parks. Which statement best explains why the collective action matters more than individual action alone?

options.label: A
options.text: Collective action is paid work, while individual cleaning is non-economic.

options.label: B
options.text: Collective action replaces individual responsibility, so each person need only participate in community drives.

options.label: C
options.text: Individual action is sufficient for a clean nation; collective action is only needed for larger cities.

options.label: D
options.text: Individual cleaning keeps a home tidy, but collective action produces a clean neighbourhood and public spaces that no single household could maintain alone.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misclassifies collective action as paid work, confusing the economic/non-economic distinction with the individual/collective distinction — a cross-concept error the chapter is specifically designed to resolve.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Underestimates the necessity of collective action by claiming individual effort is sufficient, showing the student has not grasped the chapter's argument that shared public spaces require organised community participation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reverses the chapter's logic by treating collective action as replacing individual responsibility, when the chapter argues both operate together — each person maintains their own space AND participates in collective drives.

competency.competency_text: Collect information about social institutions and organised community practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret the significance of organised community participation programmes by comparing their goals, participants, and collective outcomes.
assessment_items.question_text: Van Mahotsav brings community members together for tree plantation drives. What is the primary goal that distinguishes Van Mahotsav from the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan?

options.label: A
options.text: Van Mahotsav aims at promoting awareness about the value of trees and the conservation of forests through plantation drives, while Swachh Bharat Abhiyan aims at collective cleanliness of homes, streets, and public spaces.

options.label: B
options.text: Van Mahotsav focuses on earning wages for plantation work, while Swachh Bharat Abhiyan is entirely voluntary.

options.label: C
options.text: Van Mahotsav is a government programme run by officials, while Swachh Bharat Abhiyan depends entirely on individual citizens.

options.label: D
options.text: Van Mahotsav is a religious festival, while Swachh Bharat Abhiyan is a civic programme.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces wage-earning into Van Mahotsav, misclassifying it as an economic activity rather than a community non-economic practice, showing confusion about the chapter's classification of organised community participation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Incorrectly attributes Van Mahotsav to government officials and misrepresents Swachh Bharat Abhiyan as purely individual, ignoring both programmes' community-participation character as described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misidentifies Van Mahotsav as a religious festival, possibly confusing its festive name with the religious festivals discussed elsewhere in the chapter (langars, prasād), rather than recognising it as a community conservation initiative.

assessment_items.question_text: Name one community programme from your school or locality that is similar to Van Mahotsav or the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan. Describe who participates in it and what collective outcome it produces that individuals acting alone could not achieve.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who cannot recall a local programme may describe a school-based collective activity (e.g., a cleanliness drive, a tree-planting event on school grounds) — the analytical requirement remains the same.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's traditions of inclusion and communal giving as expressed through social and religious institutions.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how sevā — as practised through langars and prasād — embodies a tradition of communal giving that transcends monetary exchange.
assessment_items.question_text: At a gurudwara, food is prepared and served freely to every visitor through the langar. What does this practice primarily demonstrate about sevā?

options.label: A
options.text: Sevā is a form of economic activity because it involves the exchange of food for the visitor's labour in preparing the meal.

options.label: B
options.text: Sevā is a government welfare programme that distributes food to citizens who cannot afford to pay.

options.label: C
options.text: Sevā is a tradition of selfless communal giving in which food is offered without expectation of payment or return, expressing care for every visitor regardless of background.

options.label: D
options.text: Sevā is only meaningful in a religious context and cannot exist outside gurudwaras and temples.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misclassifies the langar as an economic activity by inventing a labour-exchange element not present in the chapter, showing the student has not understood that sevā is specifically defined as service without expectation of return.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overgeneralises the religious framing by confining sevā to gurudwaras and temples, missing the chapter's broader point that sevā as a tradition of selfless service extends into everyday family and community life.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses sevā — a voluntary social tradition — with a government welfare programme, showing the student has not distinguished between community-driven non-economic practices and state-administered services.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's traditions of inclusion and communal giving as expressed through social and religious institutions.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how sevā — as practised through langars and prasād — embodies a tradition of communal giving that transcends monetary exchange.
assessment_items.question_text: Kabir's grandfather voluntarily teaches geography to neighbourhood children without any payment. A school teacher teaches the same subject for a salary. What is the most important difference between these two activities according to the chapter's concept of sevā?

options.label: A
options.text: Both activities are identical in nature because the content being taught — geography — is the same in both cases.

options.label: B
options.text: The grandfather's teaching is a non-economic activity only because he teaches fewer students than the school teacher.

options.label: C
options.text: The grandfather's teaching is less effective because he is not professionally trained, unlike the school teacher.

options.label: D
options.text: The school teacher's work is an economic activity performed in exchange for a salary, while the grandfather's teaching is sevā — selfless service done without expectation of monetary return.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Focuses on teaching quality rather than the economic/non-economic distinction, suggesting the student has not identified that the chapter's comparison turns on motivation and monetary exchange, not professional competence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Attributes the non-economic nature of the grandfather's teaching to a quantitative difference (fewer students) rather than the defining criterion of absence of monetary expectation, showing a surface rather than conceptual understanding.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Equates the two activities based on shared content (geography), ignoring the chapter's framework that what determines economic versus non-economic character is the presence or absence of money, not the subject matter.
